extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students (or general readers) studying American government / civics
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook-style overview of the structure, jurisdiction, powers, and procedures of the United States federal judiciary, including courts, writs, and judicial review. Intended to teach students how federal courts are organized and what legal powers and constraints they possess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circuit Court of Appeals: composition and jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The Circuit Court of Appeals reviews, by appeal or writ of error, decisions in the lower District Courts; its decision is final in many cases (e.g., controversies between aliens and citizens, suits between citizens of different states, and cases arising under patent, revenue, and criminal laws). Circuit judges (number varying by circuit) are appointed by the President and Senate; each Supreme Court Justice is allotted to one of the nine circuits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In circuits with heavy business there are four judges, in smaller circuits two, in others three. The Court of Appeals may ask the Supreme Court for instructions on any point of law; the Supreme Court may call up and decide a case or inquire by writ of certiorari into final causes pending in the Circuit Court of Appeals. Exceptions exist where appeals may go directly from lower courts to the Supreme Court (e.g., when involving the Constitution, the constitutionality of laws or treaties, or jurisdictional matters).

rubrics_metrics.name: District Courts: organization and subject-matter jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The District Court is the lowest federal court. The country is divided into some eighty or ninety districts; each district has one to four district judges appointed by the President and Senate. Large districts are divided into divisions with law-specified dates and places for terms of court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The jurisdiction embraces many matters, including all crimes and offences cognizable under United States authority; cases arising under internal revenue, postal, and copyright laws; bankruptcy proceedings; suits and proceedings under laws regulating immigration and contract labor; and suits under laws to protect trade and commerce against restraints and monopolies. (Historically, Circuit Courts between appeals courts and district courts were abolished and their business transferred to district courts.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Department of Justice / Attorney General: duties and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The Attorney-General is the head of the Department of Justice and the chief law officer of the federal government: represents the United States in legal matters, gives legal advice to the President and executive department heads, appears in the Supreme Court in cases of special gravity, supervises United States attorneys and marshals, and provides special counsel when required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The enforcement of important federal laws depends largely upon the activity of the Attorney-General, and historically the Attorney-General is subject to the direction of the President (example: Tennessee Coal and Iron affair, 1909).

rubrics_metrics.name: United States attorneys and marshals: roles and appointment
rubrics_metrics.description: In each judicial district there is a United States district attorney who represents the government in prosecution and defense of cases within the district, and a marshal whose duty is to enforce federal court orders, arrest offenders against federal law, and assist execution of federal law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both positions are appointed by the President with Senate confirmation; they are assisted by deputies and carry out prosecutorial and enforcement functions at the district level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal jurisdiction over particular parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal courts have jurisdiction over cases affecting ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls; controversies to which the United States is a party; controversies between two or more states; between a state and citizens of another state; between citizens of different states; and between a state (or its citizens) and foreign states, citizens, or subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the purposes of suing in federal courts, corporations are regarded as 'citizens.' The Constitution bars suits in law or equity against a state by American citizens or by citizens of foreign states (i.e., suits against a state). When these parties are involved, a case may come under federal judicial power regardless of the nature of the matter in controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal jurisdiction over subject-matter (matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal judicial power extends to all cases in law and equity arising under the Constitution, the statutes, and the treaties of the United States, and to all admiralty and maritime cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'case' arises when some subject touching the Constitution, laws, or treaties of the United States is submitted to the courts by a party asserting rights in the form prescribed by law; a federal court's correct decision must involve interpretation of the Constitution, federal laws, or treaties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court original versus appellate jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution gives the Supreme Court original (but not exclusive) jurisdiction in cases affecting ambassadors, public ministers and consuls, and cases in which a state is a party. Over all other cases within federal judicial power the Supreme Court has appellate jurisdiction as to law and fact, subject to exceptions and regulations made by Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the Constitution does not specify distribution of federal judicial powers except for the two classes above, Congress decides whether other federal courts may try such cases and under what limitations. The Supreme Court's appellate jurisdiction is therefore subject to congressional control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habeas corpus: purpose, conditions, and procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Habeas corpus secures to any imprisoned person the right to an immediate preliminary hearing to discover reasons for detention. Federal courts have the power to issue the writ; justices and judges may grant it within their jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writ can be issued only when a prisoner is in jail under federal custody or authority; for acts done or omitted in pursuance of U.S. law or federal court order; when detained in violation of the Constitution or U.S. law or treaty; or for foreign citizens claiming imprisonment for acts sanctioned by their government. Application must be a written complaint signed by the prisoner setting forth facts; the judge must grant the writ unless the application itself shows entitlement is lacking. The respondent must return and produce the prisoner; the court then proceeds summarily to examine facts and either release the prisoner or remand for trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandamus: scope, limitations, and requisites
rubrics_metrics.description: The writ of mandamus is used against public officials, private persons, and corporations to compel performance of a duty required by law; it is properly used against executive officers to compel performance of ministerial duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandamus will not issue to control or direct a purely discretionary act (where performance depends on official pleasure or interpretation of law). The petitioner must show that there is no other adequate legal remedy and that he has a clear legal right to have the action performed. It is also often used to compel an inferior court to act on matters within its jurisdiction which it has refused to hear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunctions: types, uses, and procedural safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction (or bill of injunction) may be mandatory (ordering performance), a temporary restraining order (forbidding alteration of existing condition), or a permanent injunction (prohibiting acts not remediable at law). It is often used to preserve status quo or prevent irreparable injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Injunctions have been commonly issued in labor disputes and cases involving interference with interstate commerce or the mails. Political controversy arose over alleged hasty or arbitrary injunctions. Proposed procedural reforms (Republican platform, Taft's recommendation) call for statutory limits: no injunction or temporary restraining order should be issued without notice (except where delay would cause irreparable injury), a speedy hearing thereafter, and written findings on the record defining the injury, why it is irreparable, and the date/time of issuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review: authority to pass upon constitutionality and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the Constitution does not expressly provide that courts may declare statutes invalid, Chief Justice Marshall in Marbury v. Madison established that courts possess the power to declare statutes void when they conflict with fundamental law. Congress has provided procedures for testing constitutionality in the Supreme Court (e.g., appeals from state courts when federal rights are claimed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal courts will not consider constitutionality in the abstract or render advisory opinions to Congress or the President; they decide constitutional questions only in the context of a case properly brought. The Supreme Court generally will not declare a law void except when there is no doubt as to its unconstitutionality; historically, the Court invalidated relatively few acts of Congress but many state statutes. Example: the Lockner (Lochner) case where the Supreme Court declared a New York law void in a case brought by a baker claiming federal constitutional rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special federal courts: creation, functions, and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress has from time to time created special courts (e.g., Court of Claims, a judicial system for the District of Columbia, Customs Court, Commerce Court) to handle particular subject-matter or regional judicial needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court of Claims hears claims against the federal government (composed of a chief justice and associates); it may decide sums due but cannot itself order payment—payment depends upon congressional appropriations. The Customs Court was created for customs jurisdiction; the Commerce Court (created 1910) was abolished in 1913. These special courts partially relieve Congress and general federal courts of specialized caseloads.
